patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm: free the swap slot of a dirty swapin folio

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm: free the swap slot of a dirty swapin folio

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch optimizes Linux kernel memory management by freeing the swap slot of a dirty swapin folio when it's loaded from zswap, which reduces the cost of exit time and improves system performance. The patch addresses an issue where dirty folios left in the swap cache caused significant delays during exit, particularly on large production workloads. By releasing the swap cache at swapin, the patch eliminates this overhead and results in a 15% decrease in exit time on a production workload.

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer David (Arm) suggested a more readable and simplified version of the condition, but questioned whether this code should be zswap-specific, implying that it may not belong in common code.

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch does not handle the case where a dirty swapin folio is reclaimed, which can lead to a memory leak.

Reviewer noted that do_swap_page() can find a dirty folio in the swap cache due to various reasons, not just zswap, and requested consideration of these cases.
sentiment_signals: zswap is simply the common case
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi David,

On Thu, Nov 26, 2026 at 1:54 PM David Hildenbrand (Arm)
<david@kernel.org> wrote:

---

I am mostly interested in the zswap benefits, but nothing is zswap
specific here: do_swap_page() can also find a dirty folio in the swap
cache when reclaim bailed out before writeout, or when the swap write
failed. In all those cases, the copy in the slot is stale, so the slot
only reserves swap space. zswap is simply the common case, since
zswap_load() dirties the folio.

What do you think?

Thanks,

Alex

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer David questioned the generality of the patch description and suggested that it should focus solely on zswap, also recommending additional measurements without zswap. He pointed out a potential issue with the 'folio is dirty' condition being linked to exclusive access, and proposed an alternative condition for freeing the swap cache.
review_comments.raw_body:
If it's generic, then the comment shouldn't mention zswap in the comment :)

And the patch description should be all about zswap.

And we should measure the effect without zswap.

So, folio dirty -> We'd need another writeback because the content on disk is stale.

If we reclaim swap, the next reclaim run will have to re-allocate one.


But why is this "is dirty" linked to exclusive?

What if we did

/*
 * Free the swapcache if the folio is already dirty, or if we will dirty it
 * immediately afterwards by writing to it.
 */
if (folio_test_dirty(folio))
	return true;
return (fault_flags & FAULT_FLAG_WRITE) && exclusive;

-- 
Cheers,

David

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
reviewer noted that the patch does not handle the case where a folio is being swapped in and its swap slot is already reserved, which can lead to a deadlock when trying to free the swap cache

The reviewer suggested that the patch description should mention zswap as an example of a scenario where the problem occurs, rather than implying it's the sole motivation. They also noted that caching swap slots can lead to unnecessary pageout work in subsequent reclaim attempts and requested genericization of this logic.

Reviewer Nhat Pham suggested removing the 'exclusive' check in do_swap_page(), citing that folio_free_swap() already handles necessary safety checks.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Nov 26, 2026 at 9:20 AM David Hildenbrand (Arm)
<david@kernel.org> wrote:

---

+1. Maybe mention zswap as an example of when this can happen rather
than the sole motivation. I suspect this is a generic problem, with
zswap being a common/easy to trigger case :)

In general, seems like the whole point of caching these slots
(especially after Kairui optimized the swap allocator) is just to
avoid repeating pageout work in subsequent reclaim attempts. In zswap
case (where we invalidate the fault after page-in), that trade-off is
not worth it.

FWIW, zram is also doing the same thing:

/*
 * Always try to free swap cache for SWP_SYNCHRONOUS_IO devices. Swap
 * cache can help save some IO or memory overhead, but these devices
 * are fast, and meanwhile, swap cache pinning the slot deferring the
 * release of metadata or fragmentation is a more critical issue.
 */
if (data_race(si->flags & SWP_SYNCHRONOUS_IO))
    return true;

so we kinda already have some backend-specific logic bled out to this
location. Maybe we can genericize this in the future :)

---

I don't think we need exclusive here at all yeah. folio_free_swap()
already does all the necessary safety checks.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Nhat Pham noted that the worst-case throughput drop is acceptable, especially with SSD swap where it will be less significant due to faster IO completion and cleaner state. However, he questioned whether a reader race with a writer could dirty the page before the reader.
review_comments.raw_body:
I think this worst-case throughput drop fine.

With SSD swap, I think the number is even going to be less
significant, and furthermore it will be much rarer to hit this case.
When SSD swap IO completes, it's going to be in clean state. I guess
you need to have a reader race with a writer who wins the race and
dirties that page before the reader?

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 4/4] btrfs: scrub: size read bios to the bwlimit 10ms burst

version_history.subject: [PATCH 4/4] btrfs: scrub: size read bios to the bwlimit 10ms burst

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch adjusts the size of read bios in Btrfs scrub to be more burst-aware, taking into account the specified bandwidth limit and its duration. The goal is to avoid submitting large bios that would lead to long sleeps, which can cause pacing issues at lower bandwidth limits. Instead, the code computes a burst size based on the bandwidth limit and duration, and uses this value to determine the bio size. This approach allows for more natural pacing of I/O operations, especially at higher bandwidth limits. The patch also introduces a throttle variable to skip throttling parity reads during scrubs.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 3/4] btrfs: scrub: handle bwlimit below 512KiB
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch updates the Btrfs scrub's throttling mechanism to handle bandwidth limits below 512KiB/s. The existing implementation had a practical minimum limit of 512KiB/s due to its interval-based approach, but this update introduces a burst duration concept that allows for more flexible and efficient throttling at lower limits. At higher limits, the patch still uses the original interval-based approach to avoid excessive sleeping overhead. Additionally, it adds a wake-up/cancel path when changing the limit to improve responsiveness.

review_comments.author: Qu Wenruo
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer questioned the practicality of setting a bandwidth limit as low as 512KiB/s, citing an example where a 1GiB block group would take over 30 minutes to scrub.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo agrees with the patch's intention to improve performance at high limits but notes that the new sleep behavior may not be optimal for modern storage speeds.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo questioned the necessity of changing scrub_speed_max, suggesting it may be overengineered and that Sashiko has already reported a low-priority issue related to this part.
review_comments.raw_body:
For the bandwidth limit, I doubt if it's really practical to set it so low.
One 1GiB bg will take over 30min to scrub, which doesn't sound that sane.

---

I agree the old sleep behavior is not that good for high limits, 
especially considering how fast modern storage can be.

---

One question, do we really need to bother the scrub_speed_max change?

I think this is a little overengineered, and Sashiko is already report 
low priority problem related to this part.

Thanks,
Qu

review_comments.author: Boris Burkov (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author agrees that setting low limits is feasible for specific use-cases, such as remote disks with a bandwidth budget, and suggests extending the scrub ioctl to support narrower ranges.

Author acknowledged that the old behavior was intended to be fast on high limits and explained their motivation for changing it: to enable slow scrubs without regressing fast scrubs. They emphasized that the patch should not help fast scrubs.

Author agreed to remove the wake-up/cancel path for changing limits, considering it a 'nice-to-have' UX feature.
review_comments.raw_body:
I agree in general.

We have a use-case with a remote disk and a bw budget for bg
checking where we would like to set a low limit. If you have a small
amount of metadata and scrub the metadata bg it can be feasible to do
quite slow scrubs and get some good utility.

Would it make more sense if I also sent a patch to extend the scrub
ioctl to have it respect narrower ranges of the disk than the whole
chunk?

---

Sorry if I was unclear but the old behavior should be fast on high
limits, at least as I understand it. My motivation here was:

1. slow scrub needs to sleep for required (possibly long) duration
between IOs.
2. sleep for required duration between IOs done naively makes fast
scrub sleep thousands of times for nanoseconds, now we are harassing
the scheduler for all the sleeping/waking.
3. bring back the upper bound on how often we sleep by always allowing
the burst worth of IO.

So the point is to enable slow scrubs without regressing fast scrubs, I
don't think this patch should help fast scrubs at all. Besides making
the code a little simpler, at least IMO.

---

Yeah we can drop it, I think this was a nice-to-have UX addon. The user
can always cancel if necessary.

review_comments.author: Qu Wenruo
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Qu Wenruo noted that at very low bandwidth limits, the read-only metadata background task cannot be utilized for over 30 minutes, and suggested a more nuanced approach to setting the limit.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo expressed confusion about the term 'burst duration' and its relation to disk chunks, but did not provide a clear technical concern or suggestion.

Reviewer noted that the patch addresses their previous concern about the minimum limit being 512KiB/s due to the fixed interval size, and is satisfied with the changes.
review_comments.raw_body:
In that case, I'd argue the read-only metadata bg can be a larger 
problem, as it means the metadata bg can not be utilized for over 30min 
if using that low bwlimit.

But overall I agree for such bw limited storage, a lower and better 
bwlimit behavior can be beneficial, just don't set the limit too low.

---

Sorry but I didn't get what you mean by "respect narrower ranges of the 
disk than the whole chunk".

---

Oh, thanks a lot for correcting my misunderstanding.

Despite the changing bwlimit halfway part, now it looks overall good to me.

Thanks,
Qu

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] x86/efi: Handle EFI_UNACCEPTED_MEMORY in do_add_efi_memmap()
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch adds handling for EFI_UNACCEPTED_MEMORY in the do_add_efi_memmap() function, ensuring that unaccepted memory is correctly reported to the kernel as RAM when CONFIG_UNACCEPTED_MEMORY is enabled.

review_comments.author: Gupta, Pankaj
review_comments.summary: Tested the patch on SEV-SNP with CONFIG_UNACCEPTED_MEMORY=y and gave it a Reviewed-by and Tested-by tag.
review_comments.raw_body:
> The EFI stub reports unaccepted memory to the kernel as E820 RAM.
> do_add_efi_memmap() has no case for EFI_UNACCEPTED_MEMORY and adds the
> same range again as E820_TYPE_RESERVED. e820__update_table() resolves
> the overlap in favour of the reserved type, so the kernel never uses
> the range.
>
> do_add_efi_memmap() runs when soft reservation is enabled and the
> firmware marks any conventional memory EFI_MEMORY_SP; that takes no
> command-line option. It also runs with the add_efi_memmap boot
> parameter. A TDX or SEV-SNP guest booted either way loses the memory the
> firmware left unaccepted, and it does not show up in MemTotal.
>
> Add unaccepted memory as RAM, as the stub does. Without
> CONFIG_UNACCEPTED_MEMORY the kernel cannot accept it, so keep it
> reserved there.
>
> Fixes: 745e3ed85f71 ("efi/libstub: Implement support for unaccepted memory")
> Reported-by: Mike Rapoport <rppt@kernel.org>
> Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
> Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Pankaj Gupta <pankaj.gupta@amd.com>
Tested-by: Pankaj Gupta <pankaj.gupta@amd.com>

Tested on SEV-SNP with CONFIG_UNACCEPTED_MEMORY=y

Best regards,

Pankaj

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 0/2] firmware: arm_sdei: Fix NMI backtrace lockups on idle CPUs

version_history.subject: [PATCH 0/2] firmware: arm_sdei: Fix NMI backtrace lockups on idle CPUs

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] firmware: arm_sdei: Do not signal event 0 to a masked PE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents event 0 from being signaled to a masked Performance Extension (PE) in the ARM SDEI firmware driver. When a PE is masked, it should not receive event 0 signals, which can cause other CPUs to hang. The patch introduces a lock and flag system to ensure that event 0 is only signaled to unmasked PEs. It also updates the cpu_pm notifier to correctly handle masking and unmasking of PEs. This fix addresses issues with CPU hangs and panics caused by event 0 signals being sent to masked PEs.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about the implementation of sdei_event_signal() and how it handles event 0 signals to masked PEs. They explain that senders signal a PE only under its lock, and if the PE is masked, they wait for any pending signals to arrive before masking. The author also provides code changes to implement this behavior.

review_comments.author: YinFengwei
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer YinFengwei pointed out that the patch does not handle the case where a PE is masked due to SDEI_PE_MASKED, and suggested adding a check for this condition in sdei_event_signal()

The reviewer questioned whether the lock should be taken in a specific scenario where the panic did not acquire the lock, suggesting that it should be handled similarly to the 'else' path.

Reviewer YinFengwei questioned the use of a specific read operation in the patch and suggested replacing it with READ_ONCE() to ensure memory ordering
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Kirill,

On Tue, Nov 24, 2026 at 07:47:04PM +0000, Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) wrote:

---

If the panic didn't take the lock, should lock be taken
just like "else" path?

---

I am wondering whether READ_ONCE() should be used here?


Regards
Yin, Fengwei

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author addressed YinFengwei's concern that sdei_event_signal() could hang if another CPU holds the lock when it tries to signal a masked PE, explaining that in this scenario the other CPU was stopped and would never drop the lock. The author concluded that there is no need for a trylock because the sender has either counted its signal or never sent one.

Author responded to feedback about the potential for a race condition between loading and storing the unmasked flag, explaining that the notifier runs with IRQs off and only this CPU writes the flag, making it safe.
review_comments.raw_body:
If another CPU holds it at this point, that CPU was stopped in the
middle of signalling this one, and it will never drop the lock. The
panic would hang on it.

If nobody holds it, there is nothing for it to keep out. This runs at
the end of smp_send_stop(), after the other CPUs have been stopped. A
sender stopped after it took the lock has either counted its signal,
which sdei_wait_in_flight() waits for, or never sent one.

Telling the two apart takes a trylock, and on failure we would go ahead
without the lock anyway.

---

No.

We read the flag of this CPU, and only this CPU writes pe->unmasked.
The notifier runs with IRQs off, so no store can race with this load.

What can still interrupt it, a stop or a panic from an SDEI event or a
pseudo-NMI, does not return here.

READ_ONCE()/WRITE_ONCE() are for sdei_event_signal(), which reads the
flag from another CPU.

Left plain, KCSAN will report it if that ever changes. See item 5 under
"Use of Plain C-Language Accesses" in
tools/memory-model/Documentation/access-marking.txt.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

review_comments.author: YinFengwei
review_comments.summary: The reviewer noted that the patch does not handle the case where a CPU is panicking and trying to send an SDEI signal, which can lead to unexpected behavior.
review_comments.raw_body:
Ah. Yes. This is the key point. If it's panic and trying to do
sdei_block_siganl(), it's in smp_send_stop() on panic path. Thanks a

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] firmware: arm_sdei_nmi: Send the backtrace IPI to CPUs with SDEI masked
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the SDEI (System Description Event Interface) NMI handler to send a backtrace IPI to CPUs that have SDEI masked, allowing them to be included in the backtrace even if they are in a power-down idle state or going offline. The patch also introduces a new function `arm64_backtrace_ipi` to send the regular backtrace IPI to a given mask of CPUs. This change fixes an issue where such CPUs were reported as not responding after 10 seconds.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series fixes a lockup issue on idle CPUs caused by SDEI NMI backtraces. The problem occurs when an event is signaled to all CPUs, including those in a power-down state where SDEI is masked. To fix this, the patches prevent event 0 from being sent to masked PEs and send regular backtrace IPIs to these CPUs instead. This approach ensures that the system remains responsive even during idle states.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern that the patch does not address the issue of TF-A refusing to signal a masked PE, but a PE that masks right after the check still takes the SGI. The author explains that this is due to the handshake change since the earlier version and asks Jinjie to run the new version on HIP12.
review_comments.raw_body:
The SDEI NMI backtrace signals event 0 to every other CPU, including the
ones in a power-down idle state, where the kernel has SDEI masked. TF-A
acknowledges the SGI behind event 0 on a masked PE and never ends it,
and the PE takes no Non-secure interrupt again. Jinjie hit it on a
384-CPU HIP12, where one sysrq-l locked up the machine.

Patch 1 keeps event 0 away from masked PEs. Patch 2 sends the regular
backtrace IPI to the CPUs that SDEI refused, which wakes them.

TF-A v2.13 and later refuse to signal a masked PE, but a PE that masks
right after the check still takes the SGI. The TF-A fix is under review:

  https://review.trustedfirmware.org/c/TF-A/trusted-firmware-a/+/55414

Tested under QEMU TCG with TF-A built without that check, 4 CPUs. One
CPU masks and unmasks SDEI in a loop, through cpu_pm, the mask calls and

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author addressed YinFengwei's concern that the patch may cause a deadlock when another CPU holds the sdei_lock at the end of smp_send_stop(). The author explained that if another CPU is stopped in the middle of signalling, it will never drop the lock, but if nobody holds the lock, there is nothing for it to keep out. The author stated that telling the two apart takes a trylock and on failure, they would go ahead without the lock anyway.

The author is addressing a concern about the potential for a race condition when reading and writing to the pe->unmasked flag, specifically in the context of the notifier running with IRQs off. The author explains that no store can race with this load due to the IRQs being off, but acknowledges that other types of interrupts (stop or panic from an SDEI event or pseudo-NMI) could still interrupt it. No fix is planned.
review_comments.raw_body:
If another CPU holds it at this point, that CPU was stopped in the
middle of signalling this one, and it will never drop the lock. The
panic would hang on it.

If nobody holds it, there is nothing for it to keep out. This runs at
the end of smp_send_stop(), after the other CPUs have been stopped. A
sender stopped after it took the lock has either counted its signal,
which sdei_wait_in_flight() waits for, or never sent one.

Telling the two apart takes a trylock, and on failure we would go ahead
without the lock anyway.

---

No.

We read the flag of this CPU, and only this CPU writes pe->unmasked.
The notifier runs with IRQs off, so no store can race with this load.

What can still interrupt it, a stop or a panic from an SDEI event or a
pseudo-NMI, does not return here.

READ_ONCE()/WRITE_ONCE() are for sdei_event_signal(), which reads the
flag from another CPU.

Left plain, KCSAN will report it if that ever changes. See item 5 under
"Use of Plain C-Language Accesses" in
tools/memory-model/Documentation/access-marking.txt.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

version_history.subject: [PATCH v3 0/3] mm: make watermark checks honour ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/3] mm: page_alloc: add a watermark check that knows the migratetype
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function __zone_watermark_ok_mt() to the Linux kernel's page allocation system, which takes into account the migratetype of the request when checking if an allocation can succeed. The function is used in several places where the caller needs to know whether the allocation will honor ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests. The patch also moves the declaration of __zone_watermark_ok() to mm/page_alloc.h and makes no functional changes yet, as it's a preparation for future changes that will make the high-order check respect ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/3] mm: page_alloc: make the high-order watermark check honour ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the high-order watermark check in the Linux kernel's page allocation mechanism to honor the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT flag. When this flag is set, the check should not consider free pages from other migration types when allocating a high-order request. This change aims to prevent fragmentation and improve performance under memory pressure conditions. The patch also updates the compaction logic to take into account the new watermark check and ensures that allocations do not stall in compaction unnecessarily. As a result, the patch is expected to reduce the number of stalls and failures during 64K mTHP faults under swap pressure.

review_comments.author: Dev Jain
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Dev Jain suggested renaming zone_watermark_ok_mt to a more descriptive name, such as zone_watermark_ok_for_alloc, to clarify its purpose and distinguish it from the existing zone_watermark_ok function.
review_comments.raw_body:
zone_watermark_ok_mt is a bad name, I am having a hard time figuring out when
to call zone_watermark_ok and when to call zone_watermark_ok_mt. Let us look at
what zone_watermark_ok answers currently, according to the comment above it:

a) "Return true if free base pages are above 'mark'."
b) "For high-order checks it will return true if the order-0 watermark is reached
    and there is at least one free page of a suitable size".

So there are two uses: whether we have enough free pages, then, whether
we have enough free pages *and* we can also allocate.

So let us do something like: we have zone_watermark_ok_for_alloc. It will call
zone_watermark_ok, which will only handle the watermark computation (so this is a
refactor for the code ending at if (!order) line in current zone_watermark_ok).
Then it will also scan the freelists for the correct order, correct migratetype etc.

Then at the callsite we clearly know whether we are just looking for enough free memory,
or whether we are looking for an allocation too.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed Dev Jain's concern that the patch's high-order watermark check does not honour ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT for callers that pass a high order, specifically kswapd's pgdat_balanced(), kcompactd's __compact_finished() under defrag_mode, and should_reclaim_retry(). The author explained that these callers need to scan the entire free list without filtering by migratetype, which is not provided by the _mt() helpers. They are open to renaming the _mt() function.
review_comments.raw_body:
A count-only zone_watermark_ok() does not work for three callers that
pass a high order: kswapd's pgdat_balanced(), kcompactd's
__compact_finished() under defrag_mode, and should_reclaim_retry(). They
ask whether the zone has a free page of that order regardless of
migratetype. They need the free list scan without the migratetype
filter, so neither of your two helpers fits them.

So the split is not count vs scan. It is the zone as a whole vs one
request, as the comment above __zone_watermark_ok() says. The _mt variant
is the one that takes the request's migratetype. Callers that only want
the count already pass order 0.

I am not particularly tied to the _mt() name, but _for_alloc() is a
mouthful.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

review_comments.author: Dev Jain
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Dev Jain clarified that they wanted to enforce the same rules as below the if (!order) check in __zone_watermark_ok() for ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests, regarding migratetypes and orders while scanning freelists.

Reviewer Dev Jain expressed concern that the patch introduces inconsistency by using both alloc_flags and migratetype to determine the allocation context, which can lead to confusion in existing callers.
review_comments.raw_body:
I think my wording was unclear. By "correct migratetype etc." I did not mean
"only the requested migratetype". I meant the same rules being enforced
below the if (!order) check in current __zone_watermark_ok(), in relation
to the migratetypes and orders while scanning the freelists.

---

Although I thought a lot last week and my approach would cause more churn due
to changing lots of places to _for_alloc, so I am fine with your approach for
now. But read on.

Currently you pass migratetype and you say in the comment in patch 1:

"Use __zone_watermark_ok_mt() instead to check whether a particular allocation
can be served."

But, for the existing callers who pass order > 0 , aren't they also checking
whether the allocation can be served? It is confusing me that both alloc_flags
and migratetype are logically part of the "allocation context" but some
callers are doing alloc_flags & ~ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT ... I am not sure whether
the below Sashiko report is related to that, I didn't check in detail:

https://sashiko.dev/#/patchset/20261116125103.2894162-1-kas%40kernel.org

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author addressed Dev Jain's concern that kswapd and kcompactd should not consider other migratetypes' free lists when determining whether to wake up or compact, explaining that these functions do not have an allocation to serve and thus do not need to consider migratetypes.

Author acknowledged that should_reclaim_retry() is responsible for clearing a flag, not the high-order watermark check, and explained that filtering by migratetype would introduce a new behavior change.
review_comments.raw_body:
No. kswapd's pgdat_balanced() and kcompactd's __compact_finished() have
no allocation to serve. They are woken with an order and balance the
zone for it. There is no migratetype to pass.

should_reclaim_retry() has an allocation, but it asks whether it could
succeed once everything reclaimable is freed, not whether it can be
served now. Its order-0 part already counts reclaimable pages as free.

---

Only should_reclaim_retry() clears it, and that is what Sashiko flagged.
It keeps what the check did there before the series: it never filtered
by migratetype.

Filtering would send movable order-2/3 requests, like 16K/32K mTHP
faults in a MADV_HUGEPAGE region, to compaction retries and the fallback
sooner. That is a behaviour change of its own and needs its own numbers.
Out-of-scope for the patchset.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/3] mm: vmscan: tell direct reclaim the allocation is ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the direct reclaim process in Linux to pass the allocation's flags down to try_to_free_pages(). Specifically, it records ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT in scan_control and uses this information to determine whether a costly order can succeed. This change is intended to improve performance by allowing direct reclaim to take advantage of free pages that are not movable or reclaimable. The patch was tested on Dev Jain's 64K mTHP benchmark and showed improved results, freeing more pages during direct reclaim with defrag_mode enabled.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue caused by the high-order watermark check not honouring the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT flag in memory pressure situations. The check currently counts free pages of every migratetype, leading to incorrect results and stalls in compaction. The patches modify the watermark checks to take into account the request's migratetype and skip free lists that cannot be used. This is achieved by passing the alloc_flags to try_to_free_pages() and modifying the should_reclaim_retry() function. The changes are based on a benchmark that shows significant improvements in performance, with 64K mTHP faults under memory pressure stalling 18 times less often than without the patch series.
